summary: Azelnidipine is a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker used for hypertension, approved in Japan (PMDA) and several Asian countries including India - it is NOT FDA-approved (this record is based on PMDA/Indian sources and is pending clinical review). The usual dose is 8-16 mg orally once daily, taken after food. Distinct among dihydropyridines, it has a slow onset and long duration of action and produces relatively little reflex tachycardia (it tends to lower or not increase heart rate), attributed to high lipophilicity and sustained receptor occupancy. It is metabolised by CYP3A4, so strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and grapefruit juice should be avoided. It is contraindicated in pregnancy.

moa: Azelnidipine is a dihydropyridine calcium-channel antagonist that selectively binds the L-type voltage-gated calcium channels of vascular smooth muscle, inhibiting calcium influx and causing peripheral arteriolar vasodilation, which reduces total peripheral resistance and lowers blood pressure. Its high lipophilicity and slow dissociation from the channel give a gradual onset and prolonged, smooth antihypertensive effect over 24 hours. Unlike many dihydropyridines, azelnidipine does not provoke - and may reduce - reflex tachycardia, an effect linked to its central/sympathoinhibitory action and gradual vasodilation; it has also shown favourable effects on heart rate and possible renoprotective/anti-atherosclerotic properties in studies.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to azelnidipine or excipients
Concomitant use with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as azole antifungals (itraconazole) and HIV protease inhibitors (e.g. ritonavir, atazanavir) - per Japanese labeling
monitor: Hepatic function in those with liver disease

preg: Azelnidipine is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women who may be pregnant; animal studies have shown teratogenic and embryotoxic effects. Women of childbearing potential should use effective contraception, and the drug should be discontinued if pregnancy occurs, switching to an antihypertensive with established pregnancy safety.
lact: Azelnidipine is excreted in the milk of lactating animals. Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment; if the drug is essential, discontinue breastfeeding.
renal: Azelnidipine is eliminated mainly by hepatic metabolism, so major dose adjustment for renal impairment is generally not required; nevertheless, use with caution and monitor blood pressure and renal function in significant renal impairment.
hepatic: Azelnidipine is extensively metabolised by the liver (CYP3A4). In hepatic impairment, plasma concentrations may rise, increasing the risk of hypotension - use with caution, consider a lower starting dose, and monitor closely. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors - azole antifungals (itraconazole), HIV protease inhibitors (ritonavir, atazanavir) (markedly raise azelnidipine levels - contraindicated/avoid per labeling)
Grapefruit juice (CYP3A4 inhibition - increased levels and hypotension)
moderate: Other CYP3A4 inhibitors - macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), diltiazem, cimetidine (increased azelnidipine exposure)
CYP3A4 inducers - rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin (reduced effect)
Other antihypertensives, nitrates, and diuretics (additive hypotension)
Digoxin (calcium-channel blockers may raise digoxin levels - monitor)
interactions.food: Take after food - food increases absorption/exposure; keep timing consistent
interactions.diagnostics: No specific laboratory interference of note; monitor BP and hepatic enzymes

serious: Marked bradycardia or, rarely, AV conduction disturbance

monitoring: Blood pressure (and heart rate) at baseline, after initiation, and after dose changes
Hepatic function (transaminases) periodically, especially in liver disease
Dental hygiene (gingival hyperplasia with long-term use)
counsel: Take once a day after a meal, at about the same time each day
Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice (they can raise the drug level and lower your blood pressure too much)
You may notice ankle/leg swelling, flushing, or headache - tell your doctor if troublesome
Stand up slowly to avoid dizziness, especially at first
Do not stop the medicine suddenly without advice
Tell your doctor if you become pregnant or plan to - this medicine must not be used in pregnancy
Maintain good dental hygiene and report gum swelling

pearls: NOT FDA-approved; approved in Japan (PMDA) and India - this record is based on PMDA/Indian labeling and is pending clinical review.
Long-acting, highly lipophilic dihydropyridine with slow onset and a smooth 24-hour effect - notable for little or no reflex tachycardia (may lower heart rate), unlike many DHPs.
Metabolised by CYP3A4 - contraindicated/avoid with strong inhibitors (azole antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors) and avoid grapefruit juice.
Contraindicated in pregnancy; often used in fixed-dose combination with an ARB (e.g. olmesartan) in Asian markets.
Class effects to counsel on: peripheral edema, flushing, headache, and gingival hyperplasia with long-term use.
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember on the same day, after food. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and continue your usual schedule - do not double up. If you miss several doses, contact your prescriber as blood pressure may rise.
overdose: Overdose causes excessive peripheral vasodilation with marked and prolonged hypotension, reflex tachycardia (though azelnidipine causes less reflex tachycardia than other DHPs), and possible bradycardia/conduction disturbance. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive: place the patient supine with legs elevated, give IV fluids, and use vasopressors (e.g. noradrenaline) for refractory hypotension; intravenous calcium, atropine for bradycardia, and high-dose insulin/euglycaemia therapy may be considered in severe calcium-channel-blocker toxicity. Continuous cardiovascular monitoring is required; dialysis is not expected to be useful (high protein binding).
